claims.claim: In vertebrates, cAMP/PKA signaling plays a central role in regulating actomyosin contractility and localized cell protrusion in directional cell migration.
claims.source: In vertebrates, cAMP/PKA signaling is known to play a central role within different subcellular regions, including the regulation of actomyosin contractility and localized cell protrusion in directional cell migration (Howe, 2004; Lim et al., 2008; Tkachenko et al., 2011); intracellular membrane trafficking (exocytosis, endocytosis, and transcytosis) in relation to the dynamics of epithelial surface domains in developmental processes and organ function (Wojtal et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on cAMP/PKA signaling in vertebrates.

claims.claim: cAMP/PKA signaling regulates endothelial TJ with diverse actions and unclear mechanisms in different endothelial cells models.
claims.source: Moreover, cAMP/PKA signaling regulates endothelial TJ with diverse actions and unclear mechanisms in different endothelial cells models (Cong and Kong, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on cAMP/PKA signaling in endothelial cells.

claims.claim: Zygotic mutants of the PKA catalytic subunit PkaC1 (PkaC1B3, PkaC1H2, and PkaC1A13) show severe CNS insulation defects.
claims.source: We found that zygotic mutants of the PKA catalytic subunit PkaC1 (originally named DC0 in Drosophila), namely, the two null alleles PkaC1B3 and PkaC1H2 as well as the hypomorphic allele PkaC1A13 (Kalderon and Rubin, 1988), show severe CNS insulation defects (Figure 1A and B), similar in strength to zygotic mutants of the negative regulator loco.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dye penetration assay data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claims.claim: PkaC1 has both maternal and zygotic components, and its maternal contribution perdures until late embryogenesis.
claims.source: PkaC1 has both maternal and zygotic components, and its maternal contribution perdures until late embryogenesis (Lane and Kalderon, 1993).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on PkaC1 expression.

claims.claim: The BBB defect in PkaC1 mutants could explain the morphologically inconspicuous embryonic lethality of PkaC1 zygotic null mutants.
claims.source: The BBB defect we observe could explain the morphologically inconspicuous embryonic lethality of PkaC1 zygotic null mutants (Lane and Kalderon, 1993).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference connecting BBB defects to lethality.

claims.claim: In PkaC1 zygotic mutants, the full set of SPG is present on the surface of the nerve cord, although the position of the nuclei is more variable than in WT.
claims.source: In PkaC1 zygotic mutants, the full set of SPG is present on the surface of the nerve cord, although the position of the nuclei is more variable than in WT (Figure 1C), an effect that is also observed in known mutants of the Moody signaling pathway (Granderath et al., 1999; Schwabe et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Repo staining data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: In PkaC1H2 zygotic mutants, the overall organization of SJs appears perturbed, and their length is significantly shorter than in WT (0.31 ± 0.03 µm vs. 0.57 ± 0.07 µm, p=0.000457).
claims.source: In contrast, in PkaC1H2 zygotic mutants, the overall organization of SJs appears perturbed, and their length, as measured in random single sections, is significantly shorter than in WT (0.31 ± 0.03 µm vs. 0.57 ± 0.07 µm, p=0.000457; Figure 1D and E); very similar phenotypic defects are observed in moody and loco zygotic mutants (Schwabe et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data and quantification shown in Figure 1D and E.

claims.claim: In WT embryos, SPG are relatively uniform in cell size and shape, and grow to form cell–cell contacts in a highly synchronized manner, with the glial sheet closed by 15.5 hr of development.
claims.source: In WT embryos, SPG are relatively uniform in cell size and shape, and grow to form cell–cell contacts in a highly synchronized manner. By 15.5 hr of development, the glial sheet is closed (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: SPG in PkaC1H2 zygotic mutants show increased variability in size and shape, and their spreading and contact formation is less well coordinated, resulting in patchy cell–cell contacts with gaps of variable sizes.
claims.source: By contrast, SPG in PkaC1H2 zygotic mutants show increased variability in size and shape, and their spreading and contact formation is less well coordinated. This results in patchy cell–cell contacts with gaps of variable sizes (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: The complete closure of the SPG epithelium is delayed in PkaC1H2 mutants compared to WT.
claims.source: Moreover, the complete closure of the SPG epithelium is delayed compared to WT (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Embryos heterozygous for PkaC1 null alleles show mild BBB permeability defects.
claims.source: Notably, we found that embryos heterozygous for PkaC1 null alleles, which are known to have ~50% of wildtype PkaC1 activity, show mild BBB permeability defects (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dye penetration assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: The dye penetration defects of PkaC1 heterozygous mutants are significantly reduced by removing one genomic copy of Gβ13F or loco.
claims.source: We found that the dye penetration defects of PkaC1 heterozygous mutants are significantly reduced by removing one genomic copy of Gβ13F or loco (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, p=0.0022 or p=0.0115); removal of one genomic copy of Gβ13F or loco on their own has no effect.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The genetic interactions between PkaC1 and Gβ13F or loco indicate that PkaC1 is part of the Moody signaling pathway.
claims.source: These genetic interactions indicate that PkaC1 is indeed part of the Moody signaling pathway.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from genetic interaction data.

claims.claim: During the larval stage, no additional SPG cells are generated, instead the existing SPG cells grow enormously in size to maintain integrity of the BBB.
claims.source: During the larval stage, no additional SPG cells are generated, instead the existing SPG cells grow enormously in size to maintain integrity of the BBB (Li et al., 2017; Unhavaithaya and Orr-Weaver, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on SPG cell growth.

claims.claim: By third instar, SPG cells have roughly doubled in size compared to embryonic stages.
claims.source: By third instar, they have roughly doubled in size and are accessible via dissection of the CNS, which greatly facilitates the microscopic analysis.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of SPG cell growth.

claims.claim: The moodyGAL4 driver becomes active only after epithelial closure and BBB sealing are completed in stage 17 embryos.
claims.source: PKA activity in larvae can be manipulated specifically using the SPG-specific driver moodyGAL4 (Bainton et al., 2005; Schwabe et al., 2005), which becomes active only after epithelial closure and BBB sealing are completed in stage 17 embryos.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work characterizing the moodyGAL4 driver.

claims.claim: Both elevated and reduced activity of Moody and PKA in SPG resulted in severe BBB insulation defects in third instar larvae.
claims.source: Interestingly, both elevated and reduced activity of Moody (moody>LocoRNAi and moody>moodyRNAi) and PKA (moody>mPKAC1* and moody>PKAC1 RNAi) in SPG resulted in severe BBB insulation defects (Figure 2A and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dye penetration assay data shown in Figure 2A and D.

claims.claim: Moody/PKA signaling plays a crucial role in the continued growth of the BBB during larval stages.
claims.source: This strongly suggests that Moody/PKA signaling plays a crucial role in the continued growth of the BBB during larval stages.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the larval BBB defects observed.

claims.claim: The BBB defects in larvae under altered Moody/PKA activity were not merely carried over from the embryo since moody driver caused only mild dye penetration defects in embryos.
claims.source: These effects were not merely carried over from the embryo since under moody driver caused only mild dye penetration defects in embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of embryonic and larval phenotypes shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: PKA is required for BBB integrity function in the adult.
claims.source: We observed the dye significantly penetrated the blood–eye barrier under reduced PKA expression compared to that in WT (1.00 ± 0.34 vs. 6.38 ± 0.37, p<0.000001; Figure 2F and G), indicating that PKA is indeed also required for BBB integrity function in the adult.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by adult dye penetration assay data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claims.claim: Upon reduction of Moody activity or elevated PKA activity, the SJ belt staining became much broader and more diffuse than in WT, suggesting extensive plasma membrane overlap between neighboring SPG cells.
claims.source: Strikingly, upon either reduction of Moody activity or elevated PKA activity, the SJ belt staining became much broader and more diffuse than in WT (Figure 2B). This suggests extensive plasma membrane overlap between neighboring SPG cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Both elevated Moody activity and reduced PKA activity resulted in thinner SJ belts and reduced membrane contacting area.
claims.source: Conversely, both elevated Moody activity and reduced PKA activity resulted in thinner SJ belts and reduced membrane contacting area (Figure 2B and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claims.claim: The mean width of SJ belts increased with elevated PKA activity/reduced Moody activity and decreased under inverse conditions compared to WT.
claims.source: The mean width of SJ belts increased with elevated PKA activity/reduced Moody activity and decreased under inverse conditions compared to WT (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of SJ belt width shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The cellular defects of reduced Moody activity match those of elevated PKA activity, and vice versa, providing evidence that PKA acts as an antagonistic effector of Moody signaling.
claims.source: The fact that the cellular defects of reduced Moody activity match those of elevated PKA activity, and vice versa, provides further evidence that PKA acts as an antagonistic effector of Moody signaling.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the matching phenotypes observed.

claims.claim: The Moody pathway regulates the organization of cortical actin and thus the cell shape of SPG during late embryogenesis.
claims.source: We had previously reported that the Moody pathway regulates the organization of cortical actin and thus the cell shape of SPG during late embryogenesis (Schwabe et al., 2005; Schwabe et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim references the authors' previous work on Moody pathway function.

claims.claim: Elevated PKA activity caused all cytoskeletal markers to become enriched at the cell cortex area, consistent with the broader membrane contacting area between neighboring SPG.
claims.source: Specifically, elevated PKA activity caused all markers to become enriched at the cell cortex area, consistent with the broader membrane contacting area between neighboring SPG (Figure 3A–D, middle column).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 3A–D.

claims.claim: Upon reducing PKA activity, all cytoskeletal markers were reduced or depleted from the cell cortex, consistent with reduced contact area between neighboring SPG.
claims.source: Conversely, upon reducing PKA activity, all markers were reduced or depleted from the cell cortex, consistent with reduced contact area between neighboring SPG (Figure 3A–D, right column).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 3A–D.

claims.claim: PKA signaling profoundly reorganizes the actin and MT cytoskeleton, which may affect the membrane contacting area between neighboring SPG.
claims.source: Thus, PKA signaling profoundly reorganizes the actin and MT cytoskeleton, which may affect the membrane contacting area between neighboring SPG.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cytoskeletal marker data.

claims.claim: PKA has been shown to affect vesicle trafficking in epithelial cells and neurons.
claims.source: Since PKA has been shown to affect vesicle trafficking in epithelial cells and neurons (Renger et al., 2000; Vasin et al., 2014; Wojtal et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2007), we investigated if PKA signaling has a similar role during continued SPG cell growth.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on PKA and vesicle trafficking.

claims.claim: Rab4- and Rab11-labeled endosomes were differentially enriched in the cell periphery when PKA activity is increased and surrounded the nucleus when PKA was reduced, as compared to their broader cytoplasmic distribution profile in WT.
claims.source: Specifically, Rab4- and Rab11-labeled endosomes were differentially enriched in the cell periphery when PKA activity is increased and surrounded the nucleus when PKA was reduced, as compared to their broader cytoplasmic distribution profile in WT (Figure 3E and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claims.claim: The major function of PKA is regulating the cell contact areas between neighboring SPGs: high levels give rise to broad membrane contacts, and low levels of PKA activity cause narrow membrane contacts.
claims.source: Therefore, our results with these different cytoskeletal and vesicle markers suggest that the major function of PKA is regulating the cell contact areas between neighboring SPGs: high levels give rise to broad membrane contacts, and low levels of PKA activity cause narrow membrane contacts, which then affects SJ organization and BBB function.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the marker distribution data.

claims.claim: In WT, the area of cell–cell contact is compact and well-defined, with a dense SJ belt covering ~30% of the cell contact area.
claims.source: In WT, the area of cell–cell contact is compact and well-defined, with a dense SJ belt covering ~30% of the cell contact area (Figure 4A, B and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ssTEM data and 3D reconstruction shown in Figure 4A, B and F.

claims.claim: Upon elevated PKA activity, neighboring SPG show much deeper membrane overlap, with areas of both cell contact and SJ coverage increasing about twofold compared with WT, but the SJ belt is discontinuous and appears patchy.
claims.source: Upon elevated PKA activity, neighboring SPG show much deeper membrane overlap (Figure 4A–E). The areas of both cell contact and SJ coverage increase about twofold compared with WT (Figure 4F), confirming the observations from confocal microscopy (Figure 3A–D), but the SJ belt is discontinuous and appears patchy (Figure 4B–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ssTEM data and 3D reconstruction shown in Figure 4A–F.

claims.claim: It is the continuity of the SJ belt, rather than the total area covered by SJs, that is essential for generating the intercellular sealing capacity.
claims.source: This suggests that it is the continuity of the belt, rather than the total area covered by SJs, that is essential for generating the intercellular sealing capacity.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the ssTEM data showing patchy SJs with increased total area but compromised barrier function.

claims.claim: Under elevated PKA activity, the mean length of individual SJ segments is significantly decreased (0.69 ± 0.08 µm vs. 2.16 ± 0.14 µm, p<0.0001), while the mean total length of SJs is significantly increased (4.28 ± 0.43 µm vs. 2.16 ± 0.14 µm, p=0.000523).
claims.source: Compared with WT, the mean length of individual SJ segments (0.69 ± 0.08 µm vs. 2.16 ± 0.14 µm, p<0.0001) is indeed significantly decreased, while the mean total length of SJs (4.28 ± 0.43 µm vs. 2.16 ± 0.14 µm, p=0.000523) is significantly increased (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of SJ length from ssTEM data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Upon reducing PKA activity, the cell contacts and SJ area between neighboring SPGs were reduced, and the SJ belt became patchy, with both the mean total length of SJs (1.49 ± 0.08 µm vs. 2.16 ± 0.14 µm, p=0.000878) and the mean length of individual SJ segments (0.67 ± 0.14 µm vs. 2.16 ± 0.14 µm, p<0.0001) significantly shorter than in WT.
claims.source: Upon reducing PKA activity, the cell contacts and SJ area between neighboring SPGs were reduced, and the SJ belt became patchy as well (Figure 4A–E). In this case, both the mean total length of SJs (1.49 ± 0.08 µm vs. 2.16 ± 0.14 µm, p=0.000878) and the mean length of individual SJ segments (0.67 ± 0.14 µm vs. 2.16 ± 0.14 µm, p<0.0001) were significantly shorter than in WT (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ssTEM data and quantification shown in Figure 4A–E and G.

claims.claim: The ratio of total SJ area to cell contact area remains constant at about 30% under all PKA activity conditions, despite the variable interdigitations between contacting SPG.
claims.source: Intriguingly, the ratio of total SJ area to cell contact area remains constant at about 30% under all PKA activity conditions, despite the variable interdigitations between contacting SPG (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of SJ and contact areas shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: SPG apical protrusions are much longer (2.01 ± 0.01 µm vs. 1.47 ± 0.09 µm, p=0.000230) upon elevated PKA activity and shorter than in WT (0.68 ± 0.09 µm vs. 1.47 ± 0.09 µm, p<0.0001) upon reduced PKA activity.
claims.source: These protrusions are much longer (2.01 ± 0.01 µm vs. 1.47 ± 0.09 µm, p=0.000230) upon elevated PKA activity and shorter than in WT (0.68 ± 0.09 µm vs. 1.47 ± 0.09 µm, p<0.0001) upon reduced PKA activity, suggesting that PKA activity more generally controls membrane protrusions and extension (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of apical protrusion length shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Cell contact and SJ area, as well as total SJ content, are monotonically correlated with PKA activity, while individual SJ segment length is not.
claims.source: Importantly, cell contact and SJ area, as well as total SJ content, are monotonically correlated with PKA activity, while individual SJ segment length is not.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the quantitative ssTEM data.

claims.claim: The discontinuity of the SJ belt is the main cause for the observed BBB permeability defects.
claims.source: This suggests that the discontinuity of the SJ belt is the main cause for the observed BBB permeability defects.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the correlation between SJ continuity and BBB function.

claims.claim: The SPG are very thin cells, measuring around 0.2 µm along the apical–basal axis.
claims.source: The SPG are very thin cells, measuring around 0.2 µm along the apical–basal axis.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of SPG cell morphology.

claims.claim: In the embryo, the hemolymph-facing basal surface of the SPG is covered by a basal lamina.
claims.source: In the embryo, the hemolymph-facing basal surface of the SPG is covered by a basal lamina (Fessler et al., 1994; Olofsson and Page, 2005; Tepass and Hartenstein, 1994), while during larval stages, the perineurial glia (PNG) form a second sheath directly on top of the SPG epithelium, which then serves as the basal contact for the SPG (Stork et al., 2008; Stork et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on SPG basal contacts.

claims.claim: The Mdr65 transporter localizes to the hemolymph-facing basal surface of the SPG, while Moody localizes to the CNS-facing apical surface.
claims.source: Consistent with its chemoprotective function, the Mdr65 transporter localizes to the hemolymph-facing basal surface of the SPG, while Moody localizes to the CNS-facing apical surface (Mayer et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on protein localization in SPG.

claims.claim: The apical localization of Moody protein is dependent on the presence of SJs.
claims.source: The apical localization of Moody protein is dependent on the presence of SJs (Schwabe et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on Moody localization.

claims.claim: Active PkaC1 is enriched on the basal side of the SPG, opposite to the apically localized Moody.
claims.source: We examined the subcellular distribution of PkaC1 by immunohistochemistry (anti-PKA catalytic subunit antibody, which only bind to the catalytic subunits of PKA dissociated from the regulatory subunits of PKA after cAMP activation, not binding to the inactive enzyme) and found that active PkaC1 is enriched on the basal side of the SPG, and thus the opposite of the apically localized Moody (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: When Moody is knocked down in SPG, PkaC1 loses its basal intracellular localization and appears spread out throughout the cytoplasm, suggesting that Moody is required for Pka-C1 polarized localization.
claims.source: Notably, the subcellular distribution of PkaC1 was indeed altered when Moody is knocked down in SPG (moody>Moody RNAi). PkaC1 lost its basal intracellular localization and appeared spread out throughout the cytoplasm (Figure 5B), suggesting that Moody is required for Pka-C1 polarized localization.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Upon reduced PKA activity, Moody loses its apical localization.
claims.source: Upon reduced PKA activity, Moody loses its apical localization (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Upon increased PKA activity, Pka-C1 appears at both sides of SPG, and Moody loses its apical membrane localization and is found at both the apical and basal membranes of SPG.
claims.source: Meanwhile, upon increased PKA activity, Pka-C1 appears at both sides of SPG as expected (Figure 5E), and Moody loses its apical membrane localization and is found at both the apical and basal membranes of SPG (Figure 5E), suggesting that PKA activity affects the subcellular localization of Moody.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Under gain of function of Moody signaling (moody>Gαo-GTP), PKA remains basally localized, regardless of Moody's mis-localization, suggesting that Gαo signaling is sufficient for PKA enrichment at the basal side of SPG.
claims.source: In addition, under gain of function of Moody signaling (moody>Gαo-GTP), PKA remains basally localized (Figure 5D), regardless of Moody's mis-localization, suggesting that Gαo signaling is sufficient for PKA enrichment at the basal side of SPG.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Apical Moody signaling is necessary for repressing apical PkaC1 protein accumulation, and this polarized subcellular localization results from the antagonistic relationship between Moody and PKA.
claims.source: Taken together, our data suggest that apical Moody signaling is necessary for repressing apical PkaC1 protein accumulation, and that this polarized subcellular localization results from the antagonistic relationship between Moody and PKA.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the localization data under different signaling conditions.

claims.claim: PKA is known to regulate actomyosin contractility by phosphorylating and inhibiting myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), which leads to a decrease in Myosin light chain (MLC) phosphorylation and a concomitant reduction of actomyosin contractility in cell migration and endothelial barrier.
claims.source: PKA is known to regulate actomyosin contractility by phosphorylating and inhibiting myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), which leads to a decrease in Myosin light chain (MLC) phosphorylation and a concomitant reduction of actomyosin contractility in cell migration and endothelial barrier (Garcia et al., 1995; Garcia et al., 1997; Howe, 2004; Tang et al., 2019; Verin et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on PKA regulation of actomyosin contractility.

claims.claim: Two MLCK zygotic mutants, MLCK02860 and MLCKC234, show moderate BBB permeability in the late embryo.
claims.source: To determine whether MLCK is required for BBB function, we examined two MLCK zygotic mutants, MLCK02860 and MLCKC234, and detected moderate BBB permeability in the late embryo (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that MLCK plays a role in CNS insulation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dye penetration assay data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The BBB permeability of PkaC1B3 heterozygous mutants can be rescued by removing one parental copy of MLCK (MLCK02860 or MLCKC234), suggesting that MLCK interacts with PkaC1 in the SPG.
claims.source: We found that the BBB permeability of PkaC1B3 heterozygous mutants could be rescued by removing one parental copy of MLCK (MLCK02860 or MLCKC234; Figure 6B). This suggests that MLCK interacts with PkaC1 in the SPG.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: MLCKC234 mutant larvae showed significant BBB permeability and a widened SJ belt compared to WT, but the phenotypes were milder than those of PKA overactivity.
claims.source: Finally, we examined BBB insulation and SJ defects of MLCK zygotic mutant larva (MLCKC234). MLCKC234 mutant larvae showed significant BBB permeability and a widened SJ belt (Figure 6C–F) compared to WT (Figure 2B), but the phenotypes were milder than those of PKA overactivity (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dye penetration and SJ morphology data shown in Figure 6C–F.

claims.claim: PKA is known to phosphorylate and inhibit the small GTPase Rho1, which reduces the activity of its effector Rho kinase (ROK), ultimately resulting in decreased MLC phosphorylation and actomyosin contractility.
claims.source: PKA is also known to phosphorylate and inhibit the small GTPase Rho1, which reduces the activity of its effector Rho kinase (ROK), ultimately resulting in decreased MLC phosphorylation and actomyosin contractility (Dong et al., 1998; Garcia et al., 1999; Lang et al., 1996; Tang et al., 2019; Xu and Myat, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on PKA regulation of Rho1.

claims.claim: RhoA activity has been shown to drive actin polymerization at the protrusion of migrating cells.
claims.source: Moreover, RhoA activity has been shown to drive actin polymerization at the protrusion of migrating cells (Machacek et al., 2009), and a PKA-RhoA signaling has been suggested to act as a protrusion-retraction pacemaker at the leading edge of the migrating cells (Tkachenko et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on RhoA in cell migration.

claims.claim: Two loss-of-function alleles of Rho1, the hypomorphic allele Rho11B and the null allele Rho1E.3.10, showed dye penetration defects as homozygous zygotic mutant embryos, with the null allele showing a particularly pronounced effect.
claims.source: Two loss-of-function alleles, the hypomorphic allele Rho11B (Magie and Parkhurst, 2005) and the null allele Rho1E.3.10, showed dye penetration defects as homozygous zygotic mutant embryos, with the null allele showing a particularly pronounced effect (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dye penetration assay data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: At the larval stage, the SPG-specific Rho1 knockdown (moody>Rho1 RNAi) resulted in strong dye penetration into the nerve cord.
claims.source: At the larval stage, the SPG-specific Rho1 knockdown (moody>Rho1 RNAi) resulted in strong dye penetration into the nerve cord (Figure 6C and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dye penetration assay data shown in Figure 6C and E.

claims.claim: Rho1 is required for the formation and continued growth of the BBB.
claims.source: These results suggest that Rho1 is required for the formation and continued growth of the BBB.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the BBB defects in Rho1 mutants.

claims.claim: The embryonic dye penetration defects of PkaC1 heterozygous mutants (PkaC1B3) were significantly reduced by removing one genomic copy of the Rho1 null allele (Rho1E.3.10), but not by removing one copy of the hypomorphic allele Rho11B.
claims.source: We again asked whether PKA and Rho1 function in the same pathway and performed dominant genetic interaction experiments using a sensitized genetic background. The embryonic dye penetration defects of PkaC1 heterozygous mutants (PkaC1B3) were significantly reduced by removing one genomic copy of the Rho1 null allele (Rho1E.3.10), but not by removing one copy of the hypomorphic allele Rho11B (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Rho1 is a PKA target in BBB regulation.
claims.source: These findings suggest that Rho1 is a PKA target in BBB regulation.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the genetic interaction data.

claims.claim: PKA suppresses actomyosin contractility in a two-pronged fashion by negatively regulating both MLCK and Rho1.
claims.source: Collectively, our results indicate that PKA suppresses actomyosin contractility in a two-pronged fashion by negatively regulating both MLCK and Rho1.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the genetic interaction data with MLCK and Rho1.

claims.claim: The total cell contact and SJ areas are a major function of PKA activity: low levels of activity cause narrow contacts, and high levels give rise to broad contacts.
claims.source: Our results from modulating PKA activity suggest that the total cell contact and SJ areas are a major function of PKA activity: low levels of activity cause narrow contacts, and high levels give rise to broad contacts.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the morphological data at different PKA activity levels.

claims.claim: The modulation of the SPG membrane overlap by PKA proceeds, at least in part, through the regulation of actomyosin contractility, involving the phosphorylation targets MLCK and Rho1.
claims.source: Our experiments demonstrate that the modulation of the SPG membrane overlap by PKA proceeds, at least in part, through the regulation of actomyosin contractility, and that this involves the phosphorylation targets MLCK and Rho1.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the genetic interaction data and known PKA targets.

claims.claim: Crucial characteristics of PKA signaling are conserved across eukaryotic organisms.
claims.source: This suggests that crucial characteristics of PKA signaling are conserved across eukaryotic organisms (Bauman et al., 2004; Marks and Kalderon, 2011; Park et al., 2000; Taylor et al., 1990).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on PKA conservation.

claims.claim: Across different PKA activity levels, the ratio of SJ areas to the total cell contact area remained constant at about 30%.
claims.source: Across different PKA activity levels, the ratio of SJ areas to the total cell contact area remained constant at about 30%.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification from ssTEM data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: The proportionality between SJ area and cell contact area suggests a mechanism that couples cell contact with SJ formation.
claims.source: This proportionality suggests a mechanism that couples cell contact with SJ formation.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the constant ratio observed.

claims.claim: The primary role of Moody/PKA in SJ formation appears to be the control of membrane contacting area between neighboring cells.
claims.source: The primary role of Moody/PKA appears in this process to be the control of membrane contacting area between neighboring cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the morphological data.

claims.claim: Membrane contact precedes and is necessary for the appearance of SJs.
claims.source: This is consistent with the results of a temporal analysis of epithelium formation and SJ insertion in late embryos of WT and Moody pathway mutants, which shows that membrane contact precedes and is necessary for the appearance of SJs (Schwabe et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on temporal analysis of SJ formation.

claims.claim: The surface area that SJs occupy does not exceed a specific ratio, irrespective of the absolute area of cell contact, suggesting an intrinsic, possibly steric limitation in how much junction can be fitted into a given cell contact space.
claims.source: The finding that the surface area that SJs occupy did not exceed a specific ratio, irrespective of the absolute area of cell contact, suggests an intrinsic, possibly steric limitation in how much junction can be fitted into a given cell contact space.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the constant ratio observed.

claims.claim: The total area covered by SJs and the length of individual contiguous SJ segments are independent parameters.
claims.source: Our ssTEM-based 3D reconstruction thus demonstrates that the total area covered by SJs and the length of individual contiguous SJ segments are independent parameters.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the ssTEM data showing different relationships between these parameters and PKA activity.

claims.claim: The length of individual contiguous SJ segments is critical for the paracellular seal.
claims.source: The latter appears to be critical for the paracellular seal, consistent with the idea that Moody plays a role in the formation of continuous SJ stands.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the correlation between SJ segment length and BBB function.

claims.claim: Prior to epithelium formation, contact with the basal lamina leads to the first sign of polarity in SPG.
claims.source: Prior to epithelium formation, contact with the basal lamina leads to the first sign of polarity (Schwabe et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on SPG polarity establishment.

claims.claim: Moody becomes localized to the apical surface only after epithelial closure and SJ formation, suggesting that SJs are required as a diffusion barrier and that apical accumulation of Moody protein is the result of polarized exocytosis or endocytosis.
claims.source: Moody becomes localized to the apical surface only after epithelial closure and SJ formation, suggesting that SJs are required as a diffusion barrier and that apical accumulation of Moody protein is the result of polarized exocytosis or endocytosis (Schwabe et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on Moody localization and includes speculation about the mechanism.

claims.claim: The asymmetric, activity-dependent localization of PKA has not previously been described for PKA in endothelium.
claims.source: Such an asymmetric, activity-dependent localization has not previously been described for PKA in endothelium, and while the underlying molecular mechanism is unknown, the finding underscores that generating polarized activity along the apical–basal axis of the SPG is a key element of Moody pathway function.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of prior literature and inference about the significance of the finding.

claims.claim: The SJ grows dramatically in length (0.57 ± 0.07 µm vs. 2.16 ± 0.14 µm, about 3.7-fold) from the late embryo to third instar larva, which matches the increased cell size of SPG (about fourfold).
claims.source: We found that the SJ grows dramatically in length (0.57 ± 0.07 µm vs. 2.16 ± 0.14 µm, about 3.7-fold) from the late embryo (Figure 1E) to third instar larva (Figure 4G), which matches the increased cell size of SPG (about fourfold; Babatz et al., 2018; Unhavaithaya and Orr-Weaver, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of SJ length measurements from Figures 1E and 4G, and citations to prior work on SPG cell size.

claims.claim: During the establishment of the SPG epithelium in the embryo, both increased and decreased Moody signaling resulted in asynchronous growth and cell contact formation along the circumference of SPG, which in turn led to irregular thickness of the SJ belt.
claims.source: During the establishment of the SPG epithelium in the embryo, both increased and decreased Moody signaling resulted in asynchronous growth and cell contact formation along the circumference of SPG, which in turn led to irregular thickness of the SJ belt (Schwabe et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on Moody signaling in embryonic SPG.

claims.claim: The loss of continuity of SJ segments in Moody/PKA mutants may result from unsynchronized expansion of the cell contact area and an ensuing erratic insertion of SJ components.
claims.source: Therefore, a similar relationship may exist during the continued growth of the SPG epithelium in larvae, with the loss of continuity of SJ segments in Moody/PKA mutants resulting from unsynchronized expansion of the cell contact area and an ensuing erratic insertion of SJ components.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the mechanism underlying SJ discontinuity.

claims.claim: SJs form relatively static complexes, so any irregularities in their delivery and insertion may linger for extended periods of time.
claims.source: Since SJs form relatively static complexes, any irregularities in their delivery and insertion may linger for extended periods of time (Babatz et al., 2018; Deligiannaki et al., 2015; Oshima and Fehon, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on SJ dynamics.

claims.claim: The idea that shortened SJ segments are a secondary consequence of unsynchronized cell growth is strongly supported by the finding that disruption of actomyosin contractility in MLCK and Rho1 mutants compromises BBB permeability.
claims.source: The idea that shortened SJ segments are a secondary consequence of unsynchronized cell growth is strongly supported by our finding that disruption of actomyosin contractility in MLCK and Rho1 mutants compromises BBB permeability.

claims.claim: Polarized Moody/PKA signaling controls the cell growth and maintains BBB integrity during the continuous morphogenesis of the SPG secondary epithelium.
claims.source: Collectively, our data suggest the following model: polarized Moody/PKA signaling controls the cell growth and maintains BBB integrity during the continuous morphogenesis of the SPG secondary epithelium.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from all the data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: On the apical side, Moody activity represses PKA activity and thereby promotes actomyosin contractility.
claims.source: On the apical side, Moody activity represses PKA activity (restricting local cAMP level within the apial-basal axis in SPG) and thereby promotes actomyosin contractility.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the polarized localization and activity data.

claims.claim: On the basal side, PKA activity suppresses actomyosin contractility via MLCK and Rho1 phosphorylation and repression.
claims.source: On the basal side, which first adheres to the basal lamina and later to the PNG sheath, PKA activity suppresses actomyosin contractility via MLCK and Rho1 phosphorylation and repression (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the genetic interaction data and known PKA targets, illustrated in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The membrane extension in SPG occurs on the basolateral surface through insertion of plasma membrane and cell-adhesive proteins, with similar behavior in epithelial cell, but regulated by a distinct polarized Moody/PKA signaling in SPG.
claims.source: Our data suggest that the membrane extension occurs on the basolateral surface through insertion of plasma membrane and cell-adhesive proteins, with similar behavior in epithelial cell, but regulated by a distinct polarized Moody/PKA signaling in SPG (Wojtal et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data and comparison to prior work on epithelial cells.

claims.claim: In analogy to motile cells, the basal side of the SPG acts as the 'leading edge' of the cell, while the apical side functions as the 'contractile rear'.
claims.source: In analogy to motile cells, the basal side of the SPG would thus act as the 'leading edge' of the cell, while the apical side functions as the 'contractile rear' (Nelson, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference by analogy to motile cells, with a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Moody/Rho1 regulate actomyosin to generate the contractile forces at the apical side to driving membrane contraction, which directs the basolateral insertion of new membrane material and SJs.
claims.source: According to this model, Moody/Rho1 regulate actomyosin to generate the contractile forces at the apical side to driving membrane contraction, which directs the basolateral insertion of new membrane material and SJs.

claims.claim: SJs have several structural and functional components in common with paranodal junctions, which join myelinating glial cells to axons in the vertebrate nervous system, and they share similar regulation mechanisms.
claims.source: SJs have several structural and functional components in common with paranodal junctions, which join myelinating glial cells to axons in the vertebrate nervous system, and they share similar regulation mechanisms (Hortsch and Margolis, 2003; Salzer, 2003; Salzer, 2015).

claims.source: The vertebrate BBB consists of a secondary epithelium with interdigitations similar to the ones between the Drosophila SPG (Chow and Gu, 2015; Cong and Kong, 2020; Hindle and Bainton, 2014; Reinhold and Rittner, 2017).

results.result: PKA is required for BBB formation in embryos. Zygotic mutants of PkaC1 show severe CNS insulation defects, shortened SJs, and delayed epithelial closure. Genetic interactions with Moody pathway components indicate PKA is part of the Moody signaling pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C37 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches: dye penetration assays (C27, C35), TEM ultrastructure (C31), time-lapse imaging (C32-C34), and genetic interactions (C36-C37). The data are quantified with appropriate statistics and controls, and the phenotypes are consistent with known Moody pathway mutants.

results.result: PKA is required for continued BBB growth during larval stages and BBB maintenance in adults. Both elevated and reduced PKA activity in SPG result in severe BBB insulation defects in larvae and adults.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 demonstrate PKA's role beyond embryonic stages using stage-specific drivers and dye penetration assays. The data show significant BBB defects in larvae (C41) and adults (C44), with appropriate controls showing these are not carryover effects from embryonic defects (C43). Statistical significance is reported.

results.result: PKA activity bidirectionally regulates SJ belt morphology and membrane overlap in larvae. Elevated PKA causes broader, more diffuse SJ belts, while reduced PKA causes thinner belts, with opposite effects matching Moody activity changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 are supported by confocal imaging with multiple SJ markers (Figure 2B-E) and quantification of SJ belt width. The bidirectional effects and matching of PKA/Moody phenotypes provide strong evidence for antagonistic signaling (C48). However, the inference about membrane overlap (C45) relies on interpretation of diffuse staining patterns.

results.result: PKA regulates cytoskeletal organization and vesicle trafficking in SPG. Elevated PKA enriches cytoskeletal markers and endosomes at the cell cortex, while reduced PKA depletes cortical markers and concentrates endosomes around the nucleus.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C55 are supported by confocal imaging with multiple cytoskeletal (actin, microtubules) and vesicle markers (Rab4, Rab11) shown in Figure 3. The consistent bidirectional effects across multiple markers strengthen the conclusion. However, the mechanistic link between these changes and membrane contact area (C52, C55) is inferential.

results.result: 3D ultrastructural analysis reveals that SJ continuity, not total SJ area, is critical for BBB function. The ratio of SJ area to cell contact area remains constant at ~30% across PKA activity levels, but individual SJ segment length varies inversely with barrier function.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C64 are supported by novel ssTEM 3D reconstruction data (Figure 4) with quantification of multiple parameters. The key insight about SJ continuity vs. total area (C58, C64) is well-supported by the observation that elevated PKA increases total SJ length but decreases segment continuity, correlating with BBB leakiness. The constant 30% ratio (C61) is a robust quantitative finding. Statistical significance is reported for all measurements.

results.result: PKA and Moody show polarized, opposing subcellular localization in SPG. Active PkaC1 is enriched basally while Moody localizes apically. This polarization is mutually dependent and results from their antagonistic relationship.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74 are supported by immunohistochemistry data (Figure 5) showing complementary localization patterns. The mutual dependence is demonstrated by loss-of-function experiments (C70-C72). However, the antibody specificity for active PKA (C69) should be validated, and the mechanistic interpretation of mutual dependence (C74) is inferential. The Gαo-GTP experiment (C73) provides additional support for the model.

results.result: MLCK and Rho1 are PKA targets mediating BBB regulation. Both show BBB defects as mutants, genetically interact with PkaC1, and are known PKA phosphorylation targets that regulate actomyosin contractility.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C86 are supported by genetic interaction experiments (Figure 6) showing rescue of PkaC1 heterozygous phenotypes by MLCK and Rho1 mutations. The BBB defects in MLCK and Rho1 mutants (C76, C81-C82) and the genetic interactions (C77, C84) provide strong evidence. However, direct biochemical evidence of phosphorylation is not provided, relying instead on prior literature (C75, C79). The conclusion about two-pronged regulation (C86) is well-supported by the genetic data.

results.result: PKA is a crucial antagonistic Moody effector that regulates SPG cell growth and BBB integrity by modulating actomyosin contractility and SJ organization through MLCK and Rho1.
results.evaluation: This overarching conclusion (C3, C105-C107) integrates findings from multiple result groups. The antagonistic relationship is well-supported by bidirectional phenotypes and genetic interactions. The mechanistic model involving MLCK and Rho1 (C6, C88, C107) is supported by genetic data, though direct biochemical evidence is lacking. The polarized signaling model (C106-C107) is supported by localization data but involves some speculation about mechanisms.

results.result: The continuity of individual SJ segments, rather than their total length, is crucial for generating a proper paracellular seal.
results.evaluation: This key insight (C7, C58, C96) is well-supported by the ssTEM data showing that conditions with increased total SJ length but decreased segment continuity still exhibit BBB leakiness. The demonstration that these are independent parameters (C95) strengthens the conclusion. This is a novel finding enabled by the 3D reconstruction approach.

results.result: PKA regulates membrane protrusion length in SPG, and SJ length scales with SPG cell size during larval growth.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 is supported by quantification from ssTEM (Figure 4—supplement 1) showing bidirectional effects of PKA on apical protrusion length. Claim C100 is supported by comparison of embryonic and larval SJ measurements, showing ~3.7-fold growth matching cell size increase. Both findings are well-quantified with statistics.

results.result: The ratio of SJ area to cell contact area remains constant at ~30%, suggesting a coupling mechanism between cell contact and SJ formation, with Moody/PKA primarily controlling membrane contact area.
results.evaluation: The constant 30% ratio (C90) is a robust quantitative finding from ssTEM data. The inference about coupling mechanisms (C91) and the primary role of Moody/PKA in controlling contact area (C92) are well-supported by the data. The support from prior temporal analysis (C93) strengthens the conclusion. However, the speculation about steric limitations (C94) goes beyond the data.

results.result: A model for polarized Moody/PKA signaling in SPG growth: the basal side acts as a 'leading edge' with PKA-mediated membrane extension, while the apical side functions as a 'contractile rear' with Moody-mediated actomyosin contractility.
results.evaluation: This model (C108-C113) integrates the localization and functional data into a coherent framework by analogy to cell migration (C109). While the polarized localization (C99) and bidirectional effects on cell contacts (C112-C113) are well-supported, the mechanistic details about membrane insertion (C108, C110) and the 'conveyor belt' model (C111) are largely speculative. The model is plausible and consistent with the data but lacks direct experimental validation of the proposed mechanisms.

results.result: Background information on Drosophila BBB structure, SPG biology, SJ composition, Moody pathway components, PKA function, and prior work establishing the foundation for this study.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C2, C8-C26, C38-C40, C49, C53, C65-C68, C75, C79-C80, C89, C97-C98, C101, C103, C114-C115) provide essential background and context, primarily supported by citations to prior literature. They establish the known components and functions that this study builds upon. The claims are generally well-supported by appropriate citations.

results.result: The loss of SJ continuity in Moody/PKA mutants may result from unsynchronized cell growth and erratic SJ insertion, supported by MLCK and Rho1 mutant phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 is speculative about the mechanism underlying SJ discontinuity, extrapolating from embryonic observations to larvae. Claim C104 argues that MLCK and Rho1 data support this model, but the connection is indirect. While plausible, this mechanistic explanation lacks direct experimental validation and represents a hypothesis for future testing rather than a demonstrated result.
